records.greek: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή, καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ὁ γεωργός ἐστιν·
records.gloss: I am the vine the true, and the Father of me the vinedresser is.

L.1: I am the vine, the true [one], and My Father is the vinedresser.

R.1: I am the true vine. My Father is the gardener who takes care of the vine.

decisions.choice: I am the vine: the last of the sayings in which Jesus says "I am" with a picture
decisions.reason: Here "I am" has a predicate, as in "I am the bread of life" (6:35), "I am the light of the world" (8:12), "I am the gate" (10:7), "I am the good shepherd" (10:11), "I am the resurrection and the life" (11:25) and "I am the way" (14:6). This is the last of these sayings in John. The "I" is stressed: Jesus himself is the vine, and the picture that follows (15:1-8) is about being joined to him.

decisions.choice: the vine: the Scriptures' picture of Israel as the vine God planted
alternatives: a picture drawn only from ordinary farming
decisions.reason: In the Scriptures Israel is God's vine or vineyard, planted and tended by him, which too often bore no good fruit: Psalm 80:9-17; Isaiah 5:1-7; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15:1-8; 19:10-14; Hosea 10:1. Psalm 80 links the vine with "the son of man" whom God made strong (80:16, 18). Jesus now says that he is the vine: the people of God are found in him, and fruit comes from being joined to him.

decisions.choice: true: real, the genuine vine to which the picture pointed
alternatives: true as opposed to false or lying
decisions.reason: ἀληθινή means genuine, the real thing, as with the true light (1:9) and the true bread from heaven (6:32). It does not call Israel a false vine; it says that Jesus is the vine in the full sense, the one the old picture was pointing toward. The Greek puts "the true" after "the vine", for weight.

decisions.choice: vinedresser: the one who works the land and tends the vine
decisions.reason: γεωργός is a general word for a farmer, one who works the soil; in the picture of a vine it means the one who plants, cares for and prunes it. The Father is the one who acts on the branches in 15:2. In Isaiah 5:1-7 it is God who planted and tended his vineyard.

decisions.choice: vinedresser (L); vine grower (B); the gardener who takes care of the vine (R)
decisions.reason: Literal uses the traditional word for one who tends vines. Balanced says "vine grower", a plain modern term that keeps the link with the vine. Readable uses the common word "gardener" and says what he does, which also prepares for the pruning in 15:2 (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}}
decisions.reason: Every pronoun for Jesus or for God uses the deity_pronoun setting, including "me" and "my" when Jesus speaks of himself, and "he" and "his" for the Father. At the start of a sentence "My" or "He" is written plain. This applies throughout the passage.

records.heading: The true vine

records.greek: πᾶν κλῆμα ἐν ἐμοὶ μὴ φέρον καρπὸν αἴρει αὐτό, καὶ πᾶν τὸ καρπὸν φέρον καθαίρει αὐτὸ ἵνα καρπὸν πλείονα φέρῃ.
records.gloss: Every branch in me not bearing fruit, he takes away it; and every [one] the fruit bearing, he cleans it, so that fruit more it may bear.

L.2: Every branch in Me not bearing fruit, He takes it away; and every [one] bearing fruit, He cleans it, so that it may bear more fruit.

R.2: If a branch in Me does not bear fruit, My Father takes it away. And if a branch does bear fruit, He trims it and makes it clean, so that it will bear even more fruit.

decisions.choice: takes away: removes the fruitless branch
alternatives: lifts up: raises a branch that trails on the ground so that it can bear fruit
decisions.reason: αἴρει most often means "take away" or "remove" (1:29; 11:39, 48; 17:15; 19:15, 31, 38), and here it stands against pruning the fruitful branch: one kind is removed, the other cleaned. 15:6 goes on to the branch that is thrown out. The verb can also mean "lift up" (5:8-12; 8:59), and some take the picture to be of a vinedresser raising fallen branches off the ground in care for them. The common meaning and the contrast in the verse favor "takes away", but the other reading is possible.

decisions.choice: cleans: prunes, with a play on "clean" in 15:3
alternatives: prunes, with no play on words
decisions.reason: καθαίρει means to clean or cleanse; used of a vine it means to clear away growth so that the branch bears more. Jesus chooses this verb, not the usual word for pruning, and then says in the next breath, "you are clean" (καθαροί, 15:3), a word from the same root. The pruning of the branches and the cleanness of the disciples are one thought.

decisions.choice: fruit: the life that grows from being joined to Jesus
decisions.reason: "Fruit" in the picture is what a branch produces because it is joined to the vine. The passage fills it out: prayer that is answered (15:7), the Father glorified and disciples shown to be his (15:8), love and obedience (15:9-12), and joy (15:11). In 15:16 Jesus speaks of fruit that lasts. It is not named more narrowly than that.

decisions.choice: cleans (L); prunes clean (B); trims it and makes it clean (R)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the word "clean", so that the reader hears the link with "you are clean" in 15:3 (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable add the gardener's word, so that the picture stays clear. "Fruit" is kept at every level: it is the key word of the picture.

decisions.choice: If a branch ...; my Father takes it away
decisions.reason: Readable names the Father as the one who acts, since the subject of the verbs is the vinedresser of 15:1, and breaks the sentence in two.

records.greek: ἤδη ὑμεῖς καθαροί ἐστε διὰ τὸν λόγον ὃν λελάληκα ὑμῖν·
records.gloss: Already you clean are because of the word that I have spoken to you.

L.3: Already you are clean on account of the word that I have spoken to you.

R.3: The message I have spoken to you has already made you clean.

decisions.choice: you are clean: the disciples already belong to Jesus and are cleansed, as in 13:10
decisions.reason: At the foot-washing Jesus said, "you are clean, but not all of you" (13:10-11), and Judas has now gone out (13:30). Speaking to the eleven, he says they are already clean. In the picture they are the fruitful branches that the Father has cleaned (15:2): the cleansing is not still ahead of them.

decisions.choice: because of the word: Jesus's message is the reason they are clean
alternatives: through the word, as the means
decisions.reason: διὰ with this case gives the reason: it is on account of the word that they are clean. The word is Jesus's whole message, which they have received and kept (8:31; 17:6, 8, 17). The perfect "I have spoken" looks back on all he has said and its lasting effect.

decisions.choice: Because of the word ... you are clean already (B); The message ... has already made you clean (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the reason first and keeps "clean" for the link with 15:2. Readable makes the word the subject, "has made you clean", a plain way of saying "because of" (meaning decision m2), and says "message" for the word as Jesus's whole teaching.

records.greek: μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: Remain in me, and I in you.

L.4: Remain in Me, and I in you.

R.4: Remain in Me, and I will remain in you.

decisions.choice: remain: stay joined to Jesus, a lasting union
decisions.reason: μείνατε is the verb John uses both for staying in a place (1:38-39) and for the lasting union between Jesus and those who are his (6:56; 8:31; 14:10, 17). It appears ten times in 15:4-10, more than anywhere else in the Gospel. The command is not to come to Jesus for the first time, but to stay where they already are, joined to him.

decisions.choice: and I in you: a promise that goes with the command: remain in me, and I will remain in you
alternatives: a comparison: remain in me, as I remain in you
a second part of the command: and see that I remain in you
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb in the second half, so it must be supplied. Most naturally it is a promise joined to the command: if they remain in him, he will remain in them (compare 6:56; 14:20, 23). It can also be read as a comparison, "as I remain in you", or as part of the command, that they let him remain in them. The two-way union is clear on every reading; the text does not settle which link between the halves is meant.

decisions.choice: and I will remain in you
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb as a promise (meaning decision m2). Literal keeps the short Greek form.

decisions.choice: remain, at every level
decisions.reason: John's word is "remain" every time it occurs in 15:4-10, at every level, so that a reader can see one verb carrying the whole passage. "Abide" is the traditional word but is no longer everyday English. "Stay joined" or "live in" would explain the picture but hide the repeated word.

records.greek: καθὼς τὸ κλῆμα οὐ δύναται καρπὸν φέρειν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐὰν μὴ μένῃ ἐν τῇ ἀμπέλῳ, οὕτως οὐδὲ ὑμεῖς ἐὰν μὴ ἐν ἐμοὶ μένητε.
records.gloss: Just as the branch not is able fruit to bear from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither you unless in me you remain.

L.4: Just as the branch is not able to bear fruit from itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither [can] you unless you remain in Me.

R.4: A branch cannot produce fruit on its own. It has to remain in the vine. In the same way, you cannot produce fruit unless you remain in Me.

decisions.choice: just as ... so neither: the branch and the disciples are compared point for point
decisions.reason: καθὼς sets up the picture and οὕτως applies it. The second half leaves the verb to be supplied from the first: neither can you bear fruit. Both halves end with the same condition, "unless ... remains/remain", so the two uses of the verb stand side by side.

decisions.choice: from itself: by its own power, cut off from its source
decisions.reason: The branch has no life of its own; whatever fruit it bears comes from the vine. Jesus says the same of himself and the Father: the Son can do nothing from himself (5:19, 30). The same phrase returns in 15:5 in another form: "apart from me".

decisions.choice: remains in the vine: joined to the vine, taking its life from it
decisions.reason: In the picture "remain" means stay attached to the vine; for the disciples it means stay joined to Jesus, keeping his words and remaining in his love (15:7, 9-10). The word that once described the first disciples staying where Jesus was (1:39) here describes a life lived in him.

decisions.choice: you cannot bear fruit (B); you cannot produce fruit (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb the Greek leaves understood (meaning decision m1) and break the long sentence. Readable says "produce fruit" and "on its own", plain words for the same picture; "fruit" and "remain" stay at every level.

records.greek: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα.
records.gloss: I am the vine, you the branches.

L.5: I am the vine, you [are] the branches.

R.5: I am the vine, and you are the branches.

decisions.choice: I am the vine, you the branches: Jesus repeats the picture and now names the disciples' place in it
decisions.reason: 15:1 named the vine and the vinedresser; here Jesus says plainly who the branches are. The Greek sets "I" and "you" side by side and leaves out the second verb. Every branch in the picture is "in me" (15:2): the branches belong to the vine and have no life apart from it.

decisions.choice: [are]
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the verb the Greek leaves understood; Balanced and Readable supply it without brackets.

records.greek: ὁ μένων ἐν ἐμοὶ κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ οὗτος φέρει καρπὸν πολύν, ὅτι χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν.
records.gloss: The [one] remaining in me and I in him, this [one] bears fruit much, because apart from me not you are able to do nothing.

L.5: The one who remains in Me and I in them, this one bears much fruit, because apart from Me you are able to do nothing.

R.5: Those who remain in Me, and I in them, are the ones who bear a lot of fruit. You cannot do anything without Me.

decisions.choice: the one who remains in me ... this one bears much fruit: the one who remains, and no other
decisions.reason: οὗτος ("this one") points back to the one who remains, with emphasis: that person is the one who bears much fruit. The short "and I in him" again leaves the verb understood (15:4): Jesus remains in the one who remains in him (6:56).

decisions.choice: apart from me you can do nothing: nothing that is fruit, nothing of lasting worth
decisions.reason: The words belong to the picture: a branch cut off from the vine can bear no fruit at all. Jesus is not saying that people apart from him cannot act, but that the fruit he is speaking of comes only from being joined to him. The Greek has a double negative, "not ... nothing", which strengthens the point. Compare 5:19, 30, where the Son can do nothing from himself apart from the Father.

decisions.choice: because: the reason the one who remains bears much fruit
decisions.reason: ὅτι gives the reason: fruit comes from remaining in him, because without him nothing can come.

decisions.choice: {{gender:them|him}} (L, B); those ... them (R)
decisions.reason: The one who remains in Jesus may be a man or a woman, so the pronoun uses the gender setting. Readable uses the plural, as at 6:56, which needs no span.

decisions.choice: you can do nothing apart from me (B); You cannot do anything without me (R)
alternatives: for apart from me you can do nothing
decisions.reason: Balanced puts "apart from me" at the end, where it falls with weight in English. Readable makes a separate, short sentence, which shows the reason plainly.

records.greek: ἐὰν μή τις μένῃ ἐν ἐμοί, ἐβλήθη ἔξω ὡς τὸ κλῆμα καὶ ἐξηράνθη, καὶ συνάγουσιν αὐτὰ καὶ εἰς τὸ πῦρ βάλλουσιν καὶ καίεται.
records.gloss: If not anyone remains in me, he was thrown outside like the branch and was dried up, and they gather them and into the fire they throw, and it is burned.

L.6: If anyone does not remain in Me, they are thrown outside like the branch and wither; and they gather them and throw [them] into the fire, and they are burned.

R.6: Anyone who does not remain in Me is like a branch that is thrown away and dries up. People pick up dry branches like that and throw them into the fire to be burned.

decisions.choice: is thrown out ... withers: past-tense verbs for what happens without fail
alternatives: was thrown out ... withered, of something already past
decisions.reason: ἐβλήθη and ἐξηράνθη are past (aorist) forms, but they follow "if anyone does not remain" and describe what happens in that case. Greek can use this form for a result that follows as surely as if it had already happened, as in a proverb. The verbs that follow ("they gather ... throw ... it is burned") are present. So the sense is a sure and immediate result, not a story about the past.

decisions.choice: they gather them: "they" is general, the people who clear dead branches in the picture
decisions.reason: The plural "they" has no stated subject; it is a general "they", meaning whoever gathers dead wood. "Them" is plural: the dried-up branches as a group, though the sentence began with "anyone" in the singular. The picture does not name who the gatherers stand for.

decisions.choice: the fire: a picture of judgment on the one who does not remain in Jesus
alternatives: the loss only of reward or usefulness
a statement of who can or cannot finally fall away
decisions.reason: A branch cut off from the vine is good only for burning, and Ezekiel 15:2-7 uses this very picture of judgment on the people of Jerusalem; compare also Matthew 3:10 and 7:19. Jesus states what the picture says: separation from him means withering and the fire. The verse does not say who in the end does not remain, and it does not by itself settle the long debate about whether a true believer can fall away. Some read it of those who never truly belonged, like Judas (13:10-11, 30; 17:12; 1 John 2:19); others read it as a real warning to disciples. The text holds out the warning without settling that question.

decisions.choice: {{gender:they are|he is}} ... {{gender:wither|withers}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" may be a man or a woman, so the pronoun and its verb use the gender setting. Balanced and Readable say "anyone who" and need no pronoun.

decisions.choice: People gather the branches (B); People pick up dry branches like that (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the general "they" as "people" and say "branches" for "them", so that no reader takes "they" to mean a group already named (meaning decision m2). Readable says "is like a branch" so that the picture is plainly a comparison.

records.greek: ἐὰν μείνητε ἐν ἐμοὶ καὶ τὰ ῥήματά μου ἐν ὑμῖν μείνῃ, ὃ ἐὰν θέλητε αἰτήσασθε καὶ γενήσεται ὑμῖν·
records.gloss: If you remain in me and the words of me in you remain, whatever if you wish ask, and it will come to be for you.

L.7: If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will come to be for you.

R.7: If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, you can ask for anything you want, and it will be done for you.

decisions.choice: ask (a command), as the SBLGNT reads
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads αἰτήσασθε, a command: "ask". Many manuscripts read a future form that differs by one letter, "you will ask". Either way, asking and receiving are promised to those who remain in Jesus. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: whatever you wish: asking shaped by Jesus's words that remain in them
alternatives: an unlimited promise apart from the condition
decisions.reason: The promise follows two conditions: that they remain in Jesus and that his words remain in them. Those whose wishes are shaped by his words ask for what bears fruit (15:8, 16). Compare 14:13-14, asking in his name, and 1 John 5:14, asking according to his will.

decisions.choice: my words: Jesus's sayings, his teaching in its parts
decisions.reason: ῥήματά is the plural of the word for something spoken. It means the same teaching as "the word" in 15:3, seen in its many sayings (compare 14:23-24). Here Jesus's words, too, are said to "remain" in the disciples.

decisions.choice: it will be done for you (B, R); you can ask (R)
decisions.reason: "Will come to be for you" means that what they ask will happen; Balanced and Readable say "will be done for you". Readable softens the command to "you can ask", which keeps the invitation in plain words.

records.greek: ἐν τούτῳ ἐδοξάσθη ὁ πατήρ μου ἵνα καρπὸν πολὺν φέρητε καὶ γένησθε ἐμοὶ μαθηταί.
records.gloss: In this was glorified the Father of me, that fruit much you bear and become my disciples.

L.8: In this My Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and become My disciples.

R.8: When you bear a lot of fruit, My Father is glorified, and you show that you are My disciples.

decisions.choice: and become (part of the same purpose), as the SBLGNT reads
alternatives: and you will be my disciples (a separate result)
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads γένησθε, a form that goes with "that you bear": the Father is glorified in this, that you bear much fruit and become disciples. Many manuscripts have a future, "and you will be my disciples", a separate result that follows. The two forms differ by a letter or two. The sense is close either way. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: in this ... that: "this" points forward to bearing much fruit
alternatives: "this" points back to the answered prayer of 15:7
decisions.reason: ἐν τούτῳ looks ahead to the clause that follows: the Father is glorified in the disciples' bearing much fruit. It may also gather up 15:7, since answered prayer is part of that fruit (14:13: the Father is glorified in the Son when he does what they ask).

decisions.choice: is glorified: a past-tense form for what is sure and complete
alternatives: was glorified, at some past time
decisions.reason: ἐδοξάσθη is an aorist, a past form, but it speaks of what happens whenever the disciples bear fruit. As in 13:31, John uses this form for glory that is certain, seen as already done.

decisions.choice: become my disciples: show themselves to be disciples, grow into what they already are
alternatives: become disciples for the first time
decisions.reason: They are already his disciples (13:35; 15:3). To "become" disciples is to be shown as true disciples by what they bear, as 8:31 says: "if you remain in my word, you really are my disciples".

decisions.choice: so prove to be (B); show that you are (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "become". Balanced and Readable say what the word means here (meaning decision m4), since "become my disciples" could suggest they were not disciples before.

decisions.choice: When you bear a lot of fruit, my Father is glorified
decisions.reason: Readable puts the condition first and drops the pointer word "this" (meaning decision m2). "Glorified" and "fruit" stay.

records.greek: καθὼς ἠγάπησέν με ὁ πατήρ, κἀγὼ ὑμᾶς ἠγάπησα, μείνατε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ τῇ ἐμῇ.
records.gloss: Just as loved me the Father, I also you loved; remain in the love the mine.

L.9: Just as the Father loved Me, I also loved you; remain in My love.

R.9: The Father has loved Me, and I have loved you in the same way. Remain in My love.

decisions.choice: just as the Father loved me, I also loved you: Jesus's love for them is of the same kind as the Father's love for him
alternatives: the Father's love only as an example
decisions.reason: καθὼς joins the two loves: the Father's love for the Son is both the pattern and the source of the Son's love for the disciples (3:35; 17:23, 26). Both verbs are aorists, past forms that sum up the whole of that love; Jesus's love for them will reach its fullest point in giving his life (13:1; 15:13).

decisions.choice: my love: the love Jesus has for them
decisions.reason: "My love" here is the love Jesus has for them, the love he has just described. To remain in it is to stay within that love and live in it, not to keep up their own love by effort. 15:10 says how they remain in it.

decisions.choice: I have loved you just as the Father has loved me (B); The Father has loved me, and I have loved you in the same way (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "has loved" for the aorist, since the love is still present (meaning decision m1). Balanced puts Jesus's love for them first, and Readable says it in two plain clauses. "Remain" stays at every level.

records.greek: ἐὰν τὰς ἐντολάς μου τηρήσητε, μενεῖτε ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ μου, καθὼς ἐγὼ τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ πατρός μου τετήρηκα καὶ μένω αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ.
records.gloss: If the commandments of me you keep, you will remain in the love of me, just as I the commandments of the Father of me have kept and remain of him in the love.

L.10: If you keep My commandments, you will remain in My love, just as I have kept the commandments of My Father and remain in His love.

R.10: If you obey My commands, you will remain in My love. In the same way, I have obeyed My Father's commands, and I remain in His love.

decisions.choice: keeping his commandments is the way the disciples remain in his love
alternatives: obedience as the price of being loved
decisions.reason: Jesus has already loved them (15:9); keeping his commandments does not earn that love but is how they stay in it. The same link runs through 14:15, 21 and 23: love for Jesus shows itself in keeping his commandments. The chief commandment is named in 13:34 and again in 15:12: love one another.

decisions.choice: just as I have kept my Father's commandments: Jesus's own obedience is the pattern
decisions.reason: Jesus remains in the Father's love by doing what the Father commanded him (8:29; 10:18; 12:49-50; 14:31). The perfect "I have kept" sums up his whole life of obedience, while "I remain" is present: the Son goes on remaining in the Father's love. The disciples' life is to have the same shape.

decisions.choice: you will remain ... I remain: the same verb for the disciples and for Jesus
decisions.reason: μενεῖτε is a future, the result promised to those who keep his commandments; μένω is present. The verse uses the passage's key verb twice, once of the disciples in Jesus's love and once of Jesus in the Father's love.

decisions.choice: obey my commands (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "obey" and "commands", plain words for keeping commandments, as it does in 14:15 and 14:21. Literal and Balanced keep "keep" and "commandments".

decisions.choice: You will remain in my love if you keep my commandments; the commandments my Father gave me
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the promise first and says "the commandments my Father gave me", a natural way of saying "my Father's commandments" that makes clear these are commands given to the Son.

records.greek: ταῦτα λελάληκα ὑμῖν ἵνα ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμὴ ἐν ὑμῖν ᾖ καὶ ἡ χαρὰ ὑμῶν πληρωθῇ.
records.gloss: These things I have spoken to you so that the joy the mine in you may be and the joy of you may be made full.

L.11: These things I have spoken to you so that the joy that is Mine may be in you, and your joy may be made full.

R.11: I have told you these things so that you will have My joy in you, and so that your joy will be full.

decisions.choice: may be in you, as the SBLGNT reads
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT reads ᾖ, "may be". Many later manuscripts read instead "may remain", the verb that runs through 15:4-10. The older witnesses support "may be". A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: my joy ... your joy made full: Jesus shares his own joy with them, and it makes theirs complete
decisions.reason: "My joy" is the joy Jesus has in his union with the Father and in doing his will. He speaks so that the same joy may be in the disciples. "Made full" (πληρωθῇ) means complete, lacking nothing; John the Baptist used the same words of his own joy (3:29), and they return in 16:24 and 17:13. This joy comes on the night before Jesus dies, and it is not taken away by grief (16:20-22).

decisions.choice: these things I have spoken: all that Jesus has said about the vine and remaining in him
decisions.reason: "These things" gathers up what he has just said (15:1-10). The phrase recurs through the farewell discourse (14:25; 16:1, 4, 33), each time giving the reason for his words.

decisions.choice: made full (L); complete (B); full (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the passive "made full". Balanced says "complete" and Readable says "full", both plain words for joy that lacks nothing. "Joy" is the key term at every level.

records.greek: Αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ ἐμὴ ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς·
records.gloss: This is the commandment the my, that you love one another just as I loved you.

L.12: This is My commandment, that you love one another just as I loved you.

R.12: My command to you is this: love each other the way I have loved you.

decisions.choice: my commandment: the one command that is his own, the heart of all he commands
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the commandment, the one that is mine", which gives weight to "my". Verse 10 speaks of keeping his commandments in the plural; here they are gathered into one. It is the new commandment of 13:34, now given again after the picture of the vine (15:1-11).

decisions.choice: that you love one another: the content of the commandment
alternatives: purpose: given so that you will love one another
decisions.reason: After "this is my commandment" the word "that" introduces what the commandment says, as in 13:34. Verse 17 uses the same construction, where it may carry a note of purpose (see the decision there).

decisions.choice: just as I loved you: both the pattern and the ground of their love
decisions.reason: "Just as" gives the measure of their love and its source, as in 13:34 and 15:9. The past tense looks at his love as a whole, and the next verse shows how far it goes: to laying down his life (13:1; 15:13).

decisions.choice: love one another (L, B); love each other (R); commandment (L, B), command (R)
decisions.reason: The same English as the new commandment in 13:34 at each level, so that readers hear it given again. Balanced and Readable state the command directly after a colon, as 13:34 does; Readable says "command", the plainer word.

records.heading: I have called you friends

records.greek: μείζονα ταύτης ἀγάπην οὐδεὶς ἔχει, ἵνα τις τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ θῇ ὑπὲρ τῶν φίλων αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Greater than this love no one has, that someone the life of him should lay down for the friends of him.

L.13: Greater love than this no one has, that someone lay down their life for their friends.

R.13: The greatest love anyone can show is to give up their life for their friends.

decisions.choice: that someone lay down his life: explains what "this" love is
alternatives: purpose: no one has greater love, in order to lay down his life
decisions.reason: "This" points forward, and the clause with "that" says what it is, as in verse 12. The verse is a general saying about any person, but it is spoken on the night before Jesus dies and describes what he is about to do.

decisions.choice: lay down his life: give up one's life freely, by dying
decisions.reason: It is the same expression as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11, 15, 17-18) and as Peter's promise (13:37-38). Here "life" means life itself, not the soul as one part of a person. 1 John 3:16 draws the same line from Jesus's death to his followers' love.

decisions.choice: for his friends: on behalf of those he loves
alternatives: in place of his friends only
decisions.reason: The preposition means for the good of someone, as in 10:11 and 11:50-52. "Friends" is a word from the same family as one of the verbs for love; a friend is one who is loved. The next verses say who these friends are: the disciples (15:14-15). The saying measures love among friends; it does not deny that God's love reaches those who are not yet his friends (3:16; compare Romans 5:8-10).

decisions.choice: {{gender:their|his}} life ... {{gender:their|his}} friends
decisions.reason: "Someone" and "anyone" mean any person, man or woman, so the pronouns take the gender setting (as in 12:25). Although the saying points to Jesus, it speaks of a general "someone", so the pronouns do not take the deity_pronoun setting.

decisions.choice: No one has a love greater than this: that someone lays down (B); The greatest love anyone can show is to give up (R)
alternatives: Greater love has no one than this
decisions.reason: The familiar wording of this verse comes from older translations. Balanced follows the Greek closely in normal English order; Readable states it positively, which is plainer. "Lay down" (Literal, Balanced) and "give up" (Readable) are the words used for this expression in 10:11-18 and 13:37-38.

records.greek: ὑμεῖς φίλοι μού ἐστε ἐὰν ποιῆτε ἃ ἐγὼ ἐντέλλομαι ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: You friends of me are if you do what I command you.

L.14: You are My friends if you do what I command you.

R.14: You are My friends if you do what I tell you to do.

decisions.choice: friends: those loved and trusted, who share in another's purposes
decisions.reason: The word follows straight on from "his friends" in verse 13: the disciples are the friends for whom Jesus lays down his life. In Israel's Scriptures Abraham is called God's friend (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8), and God speaks with Moses as one speaks with a friend (Exodus 33:11). John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom (3:29), and Jesus calls Lazarus "our friend" (11:11).

decisions.choice: if you do what I command you: the mark of friendship, not the price of it
alternatives: a condition they must meet to earn his friendship
decisions.reason: The friendship rests on his choice and his love (verses 13 and 16); doing what he commands shows that they are what he says they are, as love is shown by keeping his commands in 14:15, 21 and 15:10. The pronouns "you" and "I" are both stressed in the Greek.

decisions.choice: carry out what I command you (B); do what I tell you to do (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an ordinary verb for obeying instructions; Readable uses plain words. "Command" in Literal and Balanced keeps the link with verses 12 and 17.

records.greek: οὐκέτι λέγω ὑμᾶς δούλους, ὅτι ὁ δοῦλος οὐκ οἶδεν τί ποιεῖ αὐτοῦ ὁ κύριος· ὑμᾶς δὲ εἴρηκα φίλους, ὅτι πάντα ἃ ἤκουσα παρὰ τοῦ πατρός μου ἐγνώρισα ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: No longer I call you slaves, because the slave not knows what is doing of him the master; you but I have called friends, because all things that I heard from the Father of me I made known to you.

L.15: No longer do I call you slaves, because the slave does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, because all that I heard from My Father I made known to you.

R.15: I do not call you servants anymore. A servant does not know what his master is doing. But I call you friends, because I have told you everything I heard from My Father.

decisions.choice: slave: a person owned by a master, who carries out orders without being told their purpose
decisions.reason: The word is the ordinary one for a slave, someone who was another's property (8:34-35; 13:16). Here the point is the slave's place in the household: he is told what to do, not why. Jesus has called himself their Lord (13:13-14) and will remind them that "a slave is not greater than his master" (15:20).

decisions.choice: his master: the owner in the picture of the household
decisions.reason: In this sentence the word means simply the slave's owner. It is the same word as "Lord" in 13:13-16, so the hearers can see that Jesus is speaking about how he treats them; he does not stop being their Lord.

decisions.choice: no longer slaves but friends: the change is in what they are told, not in whether they serve
alternatives: they are freed from serving and obeying him
decisions.reason: The reason Jesus gives is about knowledge: a slave is not told his master's purposes, but Jesus has told them what he heard from the Father. They still do what he commands (verse 14), and in 15:20 he still calls them slaves who are not greater than their master. Compare Genesis 18:17, where God does not hide from Abraham, his friend, what he is about to do.

decisions.choice: all that I heard from my Father I made known to you: everything the Father gave him to tell them
alternatives: every truth there is to know
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks only what he hears from the Father (8:26, 40; 12:49-50). "All" means all that the Father has given him for them; in 16:12 he still has more to tell them, which the Spirit will teach (16:13). The past tense looks back over his teaching as a whole, while "I have called you friends" is a perfect: they are now his friends.

decisions.choice: slaves, slave (L); servants, servant (B, R); master (every level)
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, "slave" in Literal, as the style guide has it and as at 13:16 and 15:20. The style guide keeps "slave" where slave is set against free, but here the contrast is with "friends", and it turns on what they are told, not on freedom: they still serve and obey (meaning decision m3). "Servant" keeps that contrast; meaning decision m1 keeps that a slave was owned. "Master" is the word of 13:16 and 15:20, used because here it means a slave's owner (meaning decision m2). "His" refers to the figure in the saying and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: I have made known to you everything I heard (B); I have told you everything I heard (R)
alternatives: all that I heard from my Father I made known to you (Literal)
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "all that I heard" first; Balanced and Readable use normal English order and the English perfect, since the telling is complete at the time he speaks. Balanced says a servant "is not aware" of what his master is doing, which is the sense of "does not know" here.

records.greek: οὐχ ὑμεῖς με ἐξελέξασθε, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς, καὶ ἔθηκα ὑμᾶς ἵνα ὑμεῖς ὑπάγητε καὶ καρπὸν φέρητε καὶ ὁ καρπὸς ὑμῶν μένῃ, ἵνα ὅ τι ἂν αἰτήσητε τὸν πατέρα ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου δῷ ὑμῖν.
records.gloss: Not you me chose, but I chose you, and appointed you that you should go and fruit bear and the fruit of you should remain, that whatever you ask the Father in the name of me he may give you.

L.16: You did not choose Me, but I chose you, and I appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in My name He may give you.

R.16: You did not choose Me. I chose you. I gave you the task of going out and bearing fruit that will remain. And so the Father will give you whatever you ask Him for in My name.

decisions.choice: You did not choose me, but I chose you: the usual order is reversed
decisions.reason: In that time a student would usually choose a teacher and attach himself to him. Here the choice was Jesus's, as he says in 6:70 and 13:18. Both "you" and "I" are stressed in the Greek.

decisions.choice: appointed: set in a place for a task
decisions.reason: The verb means to put or set someone in a position for a purpose. It is the same verb as "lay down" in verse 13, though there it is used in a fixed expression for giving one's life. Nothing here describes a formal rite; the task follows in the next words.

decisions.choice: go and bear fruit, and your fruit remain: the vine picture of 15:1-8, now with their going out
alternatives: fruit means only their own good character
decisions.reason: "Fruit" and "remain" pick up the words of the vine (15:2, 4-5, 8). The fruit is the life that grows from remaining in him, shown in love (15:12) and in people brought to him (4:36; 12:24). "Go" adds that they are sent (17:18; 20:21). The fruit is to last, not wither like a cut branch (15:6).

decisions.choice: the second "that": a further purpose of his choosing and appointing them
alternatives: result of their fruit bearing: when they bear fruit, the Father answers their prayers
decisions.reason: The first "that" gives the purpose of the appointing: to go, bear fruit, and have their fruit remain. The second can be read as another purpose of the same appointing, or as what follows from bearing fruit. The two readings come to much the same thing: those who remain in him and bear fruit ask and receive (15:7).

decisions.choice: in my name: as those who belong to him, on his authority
alternatives: using his name as a formula
decisions.reason: To ask in someone's name is to ask as his representative and by his authority. Jesus promises that such requests will be answered (14:13-14; 16:23-24).

decisions.choice: appointed (L, B), gave you the task (R); remain (every level)
decisions.reason: "Remain" is this book's word for the verb in the vine passage (15:4-10), so the link stays visible; Readable keeps it in the phrase "fruit that will remain". Readable says what the appointing was for rather than using "appointed".

decisions.choice: the Father may give you whatever you ask {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} name (B); And so the Father will give you (R)
alternatives: whatever you ask the Father in my name he may give you (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make "the Father" the subject and supply "him" after "ask", which is normal English. Readable starts a new sentence with "And so", which keeps the link of purpose and result (meaning decision m4) in short sentences.

records.greek: ταῦτα ἐντέλλομαι ὑμῖν ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους.
records.gloss: These things I command you, that you love one another.

L.17: These things I command you, that you love one another.

R.17: I give you these commands so that you will love each other.

decisions.choice: these things: what he has just said in verses 12-16
decisions.reason: "These things" is plural and most naturally points back to what he has been saying. The verse closes the section that verse 12 opened with the same command, "love one another".

decisions.choice: that you love one another: the aim of all he commands
alternatives: content: this is what I command, love one another
decisions.reason: With a plural "these things" before it, the clause with "that" reads most easily as purpose: all his commands lead to their love for each other. It can also give the content of the command, as in verse 12. Either way, love for one another is the point of what he commands.

decisions.choice: that you love one another (L); so that you will love one another (B), each other (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "that", which can carry either sense (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable state the purpose. "Love one another" and "love each other" are the same English as 13:34 and 15:12.

records.greek: Εἰ ὁ κόσμος ὑμᾶς μισεῖ, γινώσκετε ὅτι ἐμὲ πρῶτον ὑμῶν μεμίσηκεν.
records.gloss: If the world you hates, know that me first of you it has hated.

L.18: If the world hates you, know that it has hated Me before you.

R.18: If the world hates you, understand this: it hated Me before it hated you.

decisions.choice: the world: humanity organized against God
alternatives: all people, without that sense of opposition
decisions.reason: Here the world hates Jesus and his followers. This is not the world God made (1:10a) or the world God loved (3:16), but people as they set themselves against God and his messenger (7:7; 14:17; 17:14). The word recurs six times in 15:18-19, always in this sense.

decisions.choice: know: a command
alternatives: a statement: "you know that it hated me first"
decisions.reason: The form γινώσκετε is the same for "you know" and "know!". A command fits the setting: Jesus is preparing his disciples for what is coming and goes on with the command "Remember" (15:20); compare 16:1-4, where he says he tells them these things so that they will not fall away. A statement is also possible: they have already seen the world's hatred of him (7:7; 8:59; 10:31), so they know it.

decisions.choice: if the world hates you: a real case, not a mere possibility; it hated me before you: first in time, and still
decisions.reason: The "if" assumes the condition will be true: the world will hate them (17:14). The words translated "before you" mean "first, ahead of you"; Jesus has gone first along the path they will follow. The perfect tense μεμίσηκεν ("has hated") points to a hatred that began in the past and still stands.

decisions.choice: hated me before it hated you (B, R); understand this (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat the verb ("before it hated you") so that "before you" cannot be read as "in front of you". Readable puts the command as "understand this" (meaning decision m2). Literal and Balanced keep "has hated" and "hated" as the tense allows; the Balanced past tense still describes the hatred Jesus has met.

records.heading: The world's hatred

records.greek: εἰ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου ἦτε, ὁ κόσμος ἂν τὸ ἴδιον ἐφίλει· ὅτι δὲ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου οὐκ ἐστέ, ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ ἐξελεξάμην ὑμᾶς ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου, διὰ τοῦτο μισεῖ ὑμᾶς ὁ κόσμος.
records.gloss: If of the world you were, the world would the [its] own love; because but of the world not you are, but I chose you out of the world, on account of this hates you the world.

L.19: If you were of the world, the world would love [its] own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, because of this the world hates you.

R.19: If you belonged to the world, the world would love you, because you would be its own. But you do not belong to the world. I chose you out of the world. That is why the world hates you.

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: they are not of the world, so the world does not love them
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence assumes the condition is not true, as the second half says outright: "you are not of the world".

decisions.choice: of the world: belonging to it, having its source and character
decisions.reason: "Of" here means origin and belonging. Jesus says the same of himself: "I am not of this world" (8:23; 17:14, 16). The disciples still live in the world (17:11, 15), but they no longer take their life and character from it; Jesus has chosen them out of it.

decisions.choice: its own: what belongs to it; the world loves what is like itself
decisions.reason: The Greek has a neuter, "the own thing", meaning whatever belongs to the world. The world has no quarrel with what is like it; it hates Jesus because he testifies that its works are evil (7:7). The verb ἐφίλει is one of the two Greek verbs for love; John uses both for the same love (3:35; 5:20), and nothing turns on the choice here.

decisions.choice: I chose you: the disciples' separation from the world is Jesus's doing
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is emphatic. It repeats 15:16 ("you did not choose me, but I chose you"; compare 6:70; 13:18). The world's hatred comes not from anything the disciples have done but from Jesus's choice of them.

decisions.choice: belonged to the world; love you as its own (B); love you, because you would be its own (R)
decisions.reason: "Belonged to" says plainly what "of" means here (meaning decision m2). Literal brackets "its"; Balanced and Readable supply "you" as the one the world would love, which the context implies.

records.greek: μνημονεύετε τοῦ λόγου οὗ ἐγὼ εἶπον ὑμῖν· Οὐκ ἔστιν δοῦλος μείζων τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ· εἰ ἐμὲ ἐδίωξαν, καὶ ὑμᾶς διώξουσιν· εἰ τὸν λόγον μου ἐτήρησαν, καὶ τὸν ὑμέτερον τηρήσουσιν.
records.gloss: Remember the word which I said to you: Not is a slave greater than the master of him. If me they persecuted, also you they will persecute; if the word of me they kept, also the yours they will keep.

L.20: Remember the word that I said to you: 'A slave is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted Me, they will also persecute you; if they kept My word, they will also keep yours.

R.20: Remember what I told you: 'A servant is not more important than his master.' If they treated Me cruelly, they will treat you cruelly too. If they obeyed My word, they will obey yours too.

decisions.choice: Jesus quotes his own saying from 13:16
decisions.reason: At the supper Jesus used the saying to teach humble service (13:16). Here he applies it to suffering: the slave shares the master's lot, so the disciples must expect the treatment Jesus has received. A slave was owned by a master and had no standing above him (8:34-35); "master" is the same word as "Lord" (13:13-14), so the disciples hear it of themselves and Jesus. Matthew 10:24-25 has a similar saying.

decisions.choice: they: the world that rejects Jesus, in John's story above all the authorities who oppose him; persecuted: pursued and harassed with hostile intent
decisions.reason: "They" has no stated subject: it is the world of 15:18-19, those who hate Jesus. In the Gospel the persecution of Jesus comes chiefly from the authorities in Jerusalem (5:16; 7:32; 11:47-53), and Jesus warns that his followers will be put out of the synagogue and even killed (16:2). The verb ἐδίωξαν is to pursue someone in order to harm them.

decisions.choice: if they kept my word: a real condition with a sober edge; the disciples' word will be received as Jesus's was, refused by most and kept by some
alternatives: ironic: they did not keep his word, so they will not keep yours
simply hopeful: they will keep your word as they kept mine
hostile: "if they watched my word", spying on it
decisions.reason: The two clauses are parallel. The first is certainly true (they persecuted Jesus), and the setting is hostility, so the second may be said with irony: the world did not keep Jesus's word (8:37, 51-52; 12:48). But some did keep it (17:6), and others will believe through the disciples' word (17:20). Reading the sentence as a real condition keeps both sides: as it went with Jesus, so it will go with them. The verb ἐτήρησαν means to keep, hold to, obey, as in 8:51; 14:23-24; it is not "to watch closely" here.

decisions.choice: slave (L), servant (B, R); master; 'A slave/servant is not greater (L, B) / more important (R) than his master' as in 13:16
decisions.reason: The quotation repeats the saying of 13:16, so each level uses the same English it used there, letting readers see that Jesus is quoting himself. "Servant" in Balanced and Readable and "slave" in Literal, as the style guide has it; meaning decision m1 keeps that a slave was owned. "His" refers to the figure in the saying and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: treated me cruelly; obeyed my word
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "persecute" (meaning decision m2) and of "keep" a word (meaning decision m3) in common words, and keeps "if" so that the second sentence stays as open as the Greek.

records.greek: ἀλλὰ ταῦτα πάντα ποιήσουσιν εἰς ὑμᾶς διὰ τὸ ὄνομά μου, ὅτι οὐκ οἴδασιν τὸν πέμψαντά με.
records.gloss: But these things all they will do to you on account of the name of me, because not they know the [one] having sent me.

L.21: But all these things they will do to you on account of My name, because they do not know the one who sent Me.

R.21: They will do all this to you because you belong to Me. They do it because they do not know the Father, who sent Me.

decisions.choice: on account of my name: because the disciples bear Jesus's name, that is, because they belong to him
alternatives: because they speak in his name
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person. The disciples will suffer not for their own sake but because they are known as Jesus's, just as they will ask in his name (14:13-14; 15:16). Compare Matthew 10:22 and Acts 5:41.

decisions.choice: they do not know the one who sent me: the root of the world's hatred is that it does not know the Father
decisions.reason: "The one who sent me" is the Father (5:37; 8:16-18). Jesus has told his opponents that they know neither him nor his Father (7:28; 8:19, 54-55), and he repeats it in 16:3. Not knowing God, they do not recognize the one he has sent. "They" are the same people as in 15:20, the world that rejects Jesus.

decisions.choice: but: turning from the parallel sayings of 15:20 to their reason
alternatives: a strong contrast with the last clause of 15:20
decisions.reason: The word marks a turn from what will happen to why it will happen; it does not cancel the hope that some will keep the disciples' word.

decisions.choice: because you belong to me; the Father, who sent me
decisions.reason: Readable explains the idiom of the name (meaning decision m1) and names the Father, who in John is always "the one who sent me" (meaning decision m2).

records.greek: εἰ μὴ ἦλθον καὶ ἐλάλησα αὐτοῖς, ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ εἴχοσαν· νῦν δὲ πρόφασιν οὐκ ἔχουσιν περὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: If not I had come and spoken to them, sin not they would have; now but excuse not they have concerning the sin of them.

L.22: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin.

R.22: If I had not come and talked to them, they would not be guilty of this sin. But I have come, so they have no excuse for their sin.

decisions.choice: a condition contrary to fact: Jesus has come and spoken to them
decisions.reason: The form of the sentence assumes the condition is not true. "Now" in the second half is logical, not a point in time: "but as things are", since he did come.

decisions.choice: to have sin: to be guilty of sin
decisions.reason: As in 9:41, John uses the phrase for guilt a person must answer for (also 15:24; 19:11). Jesus does not mean that without his coming they would be sinless, but that they would not bear this guilt.

decisions.choice: their sin: refusing to believe the Son when he came and spoke to them
decisions.reason: The sin in view is the one Jesus names in 16:9: "they do not believe in me". They heard his word ("spoken to them") and turned from it, so they cannot plead ignorance; this is the light come into the world that people refused (3:19). "Them" are those who reject him, as in 15:20-21. The word πρόφασιν means a plea or pretext offered as an excuse.

decisions.choice: would have no sin; as it is (B); would not be guilty of this sin; But I have come, so (R)
alternatives: would not have sin; but now (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced uses "as it is" for the logical "now" (meaning decision m1) and the inverted "Had I not" for "if I had not". Readable says plainly what having sin means and which sin is meant (meaning decisions m2, m3), and spells out what "now" implies, that Jesus did come.

records.greek: ὁ ἐμὲ μισῶν καὶ τὸν πατέρα μου μισεῖ.
records.gloss: The [one] me hating also the Father of me hates.

L.23: The one who hates Me hates My Father also.

R.23: Anyone who hates Me also hates My Father.

decisions.choice: to hate the Son is to hate the Father, because the Father is present and known in him
decisions.reason: The Son and the Father are one (10:30); whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father (12:45; 14:9), and whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him (5:23). So there is no hating Jesus while claiming to love God (8:42).

decisions.choice: the one who hates: anyone at all who hates, not one particular person
decisions.reason: The article with a participle makes a general statement, true of every case.

decisions.choice: Whoever (B); Anyone who (R)
decisions.reason: The general sense (meaning decision m2) is clearer in English with "whoever" or "anyone who", which apply to men and women alike, so no gender setting is needed.

records.greek: εἰ τὰ ἔργα μὴ ἐποίησα ἐν αὐτοῖς ἃ οὐδεὶς ἄλλος ἐποίησεν, ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ εἴχοσαν· νῦν δὲ καὶ ἑωράκασιν καὶ μεμισήκασιν καὶ ἐμὲ καὶ τὸν πατέρα μου.
records.gloss: If the works not I had done among them which no one other did, sin not they would have; now but both they have seen and have hated both me and the Father of me.

L.24: If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both Me and My Father.

R.24: If I had not done things among them that no one else has ever done, they would not be guilty of this sin. But they have seen Me and My Father at work, and they have hated Me and My Father.

decisions.choice: the works: Jesus's deeds, including his signs, which are the Father's works done through him
decisions.reason: Jesus calls his deeds the works the Father gave him to do (5:36; 10:25, 32, 37-38; 14:10-11). They are unlike anyone else's: no one has ever opened the eyes of a man born blind (9:32). As 15:22 spoke of his words, this verse speaks of his deeds; both leave his hearers without excuse.

decisions.choice: to have sin: to be guilty of sin, as in 15:22
decisions.reason: The same contrary-to-fact form and the same phrase as 15:22. The guilt is that of refusing what they have seen; "now" is again logical ("but as it is").

decisions.choice: both verbs take "me and my Father": they have seen the Father in Jesus, and hated both
alternatives: they have seen the works, and have hated me and my Father
decisions.reason: The Greek pairs the verbs with "both ... and" and then pairs the objects the same way, so the most natural reading is that the people have seen Jesus and the Father as well as hated them. In Jesus's works the Father is seen (14:9-11; 12:45). Their guilt is that they have seen and still hated. The perfect tenses describe a settled state, not a passing reaction.

decisions.choice: as it is (B); things ... that no one else has ever done; this sin; at work (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says "things" for "works" in plain words, and "this sin" as in 15:22. It adds "at work" to show where they saw the Father, in Jesus's deeds (meaning decisions m1, m3); this goes slightly beyond the words, though not beyond the sense.

records.greek: ἀλλ’ ἵνα πληρωθῇ ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ αὐτῶν γεγραμμένος ὅτι Ἐμίσησάν με δωρεάν.
records.gloss: But that may be fulfilled the word the [one] in the law of them having been written, "They hated me freely."

L.25: But [this is] so that the word that has been written in their Law may be fulfilled: 'They hated Me without a cause.'

R.25: But this happened so that what is written in their own Law would come true: 'They hated Me for no reason.'

decisions.choice: an incomplete sentence: "but [this happened] so that"
alternatives: a command: "but let the word be fulfilled"
decisions.reason: The Greek begins with "but so that" and leaves the main verb unstated, as John does in 1:8, 9:3 and 13:18. The sense is supplied from what has just been said: their hatred has come about so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.

decisions.choice: a quotation of Psalm 35:19 or Psalm 69:5 (68:5 in the Greek Old Testament)
decisions.reason: Both psalms speak of those who hate the psalmist without cause, in words very close to the Greek here; Psalm 109:3 is similar. Psalm 69 is the psalm of the righteous sufferer that John also quotes in 2:17 ("Zeal for your house will consume me") and echoes in 19:28-29. What the psalmist suffered, Jesus suffers in full.

decisions.choice: their Law: the Scriptures as a whole, which the people themselves hold sacred
alternatives: the five books of Moses only
a Law that Jesus does not regard as his own
decisions.reason: The Psalms are not in the books of Moses, yet Jesus calls them "Law", as in 10:34, where he quotes Psalm 82 as "your Law". "Their" stresses that the very Scriptures they claim to keep describe what they are doing; it does not distance Jesus from Scripture, which he says "cannot be broken" (10:35).

decisions.choice: without cause: for no reason at all
decisions.reason: The word δωρεάν means "as a gift, for nothing"; here, hatred given for nothing, with no wrong to deserve it.

decisions.choice: [this is] (L); this has happened (B); this happened (R)
decisions.reason: English needs a main verb that the Greek leaves out (meaning decision m1). Literal brackets it; Balanced and Readable supply it plainly, as in 13:18. "Law" is capitalized because it names the Scriptures (meaning decision m3).

records.greek: Ὅταν ἔλθῃ ὁ παράκλητος ὃν ἐγὼ πέμψω ὑμῖν παρὰ τοῦ πατρός, τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεται, ἐκεῖνος μαρτυρήσει περὶ ἐμοῦ·
records.gloss: When comes the advocate whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of the truth which from the Father goes out, that one will testify concerning me;

L.26: When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who comes out from the Father, He will testify about Me;

R.26: I will send the Advocate to you from the Father. He is the Spirit of truth, and He comes from the Father. When He comes, He will testify about Me.

decisions.choice: the Advocate: one called to stand beside another and speak for them
decisions.reason: The word παράκλητος was used of someone called in to stand by a person, above all in a court. Here the setting is a trial: the world has hated Jesus without cause (15:25), and the Advocate comes to testify about him (compare 16:8-11). It is the same title as in 14:16 and 14:26.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of truth: the Holy Spirit, who comes from the God of truth and makes the truth known
alternatives: a spirit or attitude of truthfulness
decisions.reason: This is the Advocate already promised and named "the Spirit of truth" (14:17) and "the Holy Spirit" (14:26). He testifies to Jesus, who is the truth (14:6), and guides the disciples into all the truth (16:13).

decisions.choice: the pronouns change with the nouns they agree with; the Spirit is spoken of as a person
alternatives: the neuter means the Spirit is an impersonal force
decisions.reason: The pronoun ὃν ("whom") is masculine, agreeing with "Advocate". The pronoun ὃ ("who") is neuter, agreeing with "Spirit", a neuter noun in Greek; this is grammatical agreement and says nothing about whether the Spirit is a thing (as in 14:17, 26). The masculine ἐκεῖνος ("that one") takes up the Advocate again and is emphatic: he, and no other, will testify. What shows the Spirit as a person is what he does: he is sent, comes and testifies.

decisions.choice: comes out from the Father: in this context, the Spirit's coming on his mission from the Father, as the one Jesus sends
alternatives: a statement about the Spirit's eternal origin within God
decisions.reason: In the same sentence Jesus says that he will send the Advocate from the Father, and that the Spirit comes out from the Father; elsewhere the Father sends him at Jesus's request and in Jesus's name (14:16, 26), and Jesus sends him (16:7). In context the verb ἐκπορεύεται ("comes out, goes out") describes the Spirit's coming to the disciples from the Father. Later Christian theology drew on this verse in speaking of the Spirit's eternal relation to the Father; the Nicene Creed of 381 uses its words, and whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son became a long dispute between the Eastern and Western churches. The verse itself speaks of the Spirit coming from the Father and being sent by Jesus.

decisions.choice: testify about me: bear witness to who Jesus is, as in a trial
decisions.reason: Testimony is a thread through John: John the Baptist, Jesus's works, the Father and the Scriptures testify about Jesus (5:31-39). The Spirit will continue that testimony before the world that hates him, together with the disciples (15:27) and through them (16:8-11).

decisions.choice: the Advocate
decisions.reason: The book uses "the Advocate" at every level, because John's setting is testimony and judgment (meaning decision m1). Other well-known renderings are Helper, Counselor and Comforter; each catches part of the sense.

decisions.choice: whom; who; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}
decisions.reason: The Spirit is never "it" in this translation. The neuter Greek pronoun is grammatical agreement only (meaning decision m3), so English uses the personal "who", "whom" and "he". "He" takes the deity pronoun setting like every pronoun for God; the relatives "who" and "whom" do not, as nowhere else in the translation does a relative pronoun take it.

decisions.choice: comes out from (L, B); comes from (R)
decisions.reason: "Comes out" is the plain sense of the verb and keeps the link with "comes" at the start of the verse. "Proceeds", the wording of older translations and of the creed, is given in a footnote (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: The Advocate ... is the Spirit of truth. When he comes, he will testify (B); I will send the Advocate ... He is the Spirit of truth ... When he comes (R)
alternatives: one sentence in the Greek order (Literal)
decisions.reason: The Greek sentence opens with "when he comes", then names the Advocate twice before reaching its main verb. Balanced and Readable first say who the Advocate is (the words in apposition, "the Spirit of truth", become "is the Spirit of truth") and then say what he will do, so the main statement is not lost; the meaning is unchanged.

records.heading: The Advocate will testify

records.greek: καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ μαρτυρεῖτε, ὅτι ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἐστε.
records.gloss: Also you and testify, because from beginning with me you are.

L.27: And you also testify, because you have been with Me from [the] beginning.

R.27: And you also are My witnesses, because you have been with Me from the very beginning.

decisions.choice: you testify: a statement that the disciples are witnesses, joined with the Spirit
decisions.reason: The form μαρτυρεῖτε can be a statement or a command. Following the promise that the Spirit will testify, a statement fits best: the disciples' witness stands beside the Spirit's (compare Acts 5:32, "we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit"). A command is also possible, and the following "because" could give the reason they are to do it.

decisions.choice: you have been with me from the beginning: a present tense for something that began in the past and goes on
decisions.reason: Greek uses the present "you are" with "from the beginning" for a state that started then and continues now: they were with him from the start and are with him still.

decisions.choice: the beginning: the start of Jesus's public work, when the disciples first followed him
alternatives: the beginning of creation, as in 1:1
decisions.reason: The disciples have been with Jesus since he called them (1:35-51; 16:4). That is what qualifies them as witnesses: they saw and heard for themselves (Acts 1:21-22; 1 John 1:1-3).

decisions.choice: testify about me (B); are my witnesses (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies "about me" from 15:26, which the Greek implies. Readable expresses the statement with the noun "witnesses", which says the same thing in plain words (meaning decision m1).
